title: ESAU MARRIED TWO WOMEN—AND HIS PARENTS WERE MISERABLE ABOUT IT
paragraphs: ESAU MARRIED TWO WOMEN—AND HIS PARENTS WERE MISERABLE ABOUT IT
Two verses. One marriage decision. A mother and father carrying grief inside their own home. And a warning about the choices we make when we want what we want more than we want the wisdom of God.
There are family wounds Scripture does not describe with shouting.
No slammed doors.
No dramatic confrontation.
No long explanation.
Just one devastating sentence.
Esau was forty years old when he married Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite.
Then Genesis tells us what those marriages did to Isaac and Rebekah:

“And they were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah.”
—Genesis 26:35, KJV
Read that again.
Not because Esau married.
Not simply because he married two women.
The text specifically identifies these women as Hittites, women from the peoples of Canaan.
And that detail matters.
The Hebrew of Genesis 26:35 says:
וַתִּהְיֶיןָ מֹרַת רוּחַ לְיִצְחָק וּלְרִבְקָה
Vattihyena morat ruach le-Yitzchaq ule-Rivqah.
The expression מֹרַת רוּחַ — morat ruach carries the sense of bitterness or grief of spirit.
Esau did not merely make a choice his parents happened to dislike.
Something about these marriages became bitterness to their spirits.
And if you have ever watched someone you love make a decision you could not make for them, you already understand something about this verse.
A parent can teach.
A parent can warn.
A parent can pray.
A parent can remember holding that child when he was small enough to sleep against their chest.
But eventually that child becomes an adult.
And adults make choices.
Sometimes choices that leave the people who love them wondering:
How did we get here?
Isaac knew something about marriage that Esau should have understood.
Years earlier, Abraham had been intensely concerned that Isaac not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan. Abraham told his servant:

“Thou shalt not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell.”
—Genesis 24:3, KJV
This was not presented as ethnic superiority.
Genesis itself will not allow that interpretation.

The issue running through the patriarchal story is covenant faithfulness—God had called Abraham and his household into a particular covenant mission, while the surrounding Canaanite world represented religious allegiances and practices incompatible with that calling.
Abraham wanted Isaac's marriage to remain consistent with that covenant vocation.
Rebekah eventually expresses the same anguish even more dramatically.
After Esau's marriages, she tells Isaac:

“I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth: if Jacob take a wife of the daughters of Heth, such as these which are of the daughters of the land, what good shall my life do me?”
—Genesis 27:46, KJV
That is not mild disappointment.
That is a mother saying, essentially:
I cannot bear watching this happen again.
Then Isaac calls Jacob and commands him not to take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.
The contrast is impossible to miss.
But something even sadder happens next.
Esau eventually realizes that the daughters of Canaan displease his father.
Genesis 28:8 says:
“And Esau seeing that the daughters of Canaan pleased not Isaac his father...”
So Esau goes and marries again—this time into Ishmael's family.
It is one of the most painfully human moments in his story.
He finally notices.
He finally sees the problem.
But his response appears to address the surface rather than undo the deeper pattern.
How many of us have done exactly that?
We experience the consequences of a decision, and instead of asking God to expose what is happening inside us, we try to rearrange the outside.
We change relationships without changing ourselves.
We change churches without confronting our pride.
We change jobs without confronting our dishonesty.
We delete the message without killing the lust.
We apologize because we were caught, but never ask why we wanted the sin.
We hide the bottle.
Erase the browser history.
Change the password.
Make another promise.
Post another Bible verse.
Smile in another church photograph.
And somewhere underneath all of it, the heart remains untouched.
That is why this ancient family story can become uncomfortable so quickly.
Because Esau is not merely somebody to observe.
There is something frighteningly familiar about wanting the blessing while resisting the God who gives it.
Earlier, Esau had come home exhausted and traded his birthright to Jacob for food.
Genesis says:

“Thus Esau despised his birthright.”
—Genesis 25:34, KJV
The Hebrew verb is וַיִּבֶז — vayivez, from בָּזָה — bazah, meaning to despise, treat lightly, or regard as insignificant.
That sentence reaches far beyond lentil stew.
Esau treated something weighty as though it were light.
Something sacred as though it were expendable.
Something connected to his inheritance as though immediate appetite mattered more.
And that is still one of sin's oldest strategies.
Sin rarely walks into your life announcing:
I am here to destroy what God has given you.
It whispers:
You need this now.
One meal.
One affair.
One secret conversation.
One compromise.
One click.
One lie.
One night.
One decision made while angry.
One relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
One appetite you keep feeding because surrender feels too expensive.
And afterward you discover that the thing promising relief was quietly negotiating for something far more valuable.
Hebrews later uses Esau as a warning.
It calls him βέβηλος — bebēlos in Hebrews 12:16, commonly translated “profane” or “godless,” and reminds believers that for one meal he sold his birthright.
The New Testament does not tell Christians to laugh at Esau.
It tells Christians to learn from him.
Because you can become so dominated by what feels urgent that you lose sight of what is holy.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You love Jesus.
Or at least you say you do.
But there is one room you keep locked.
One relationship you refuse to surrender.
One resentment you polish every night.
One addiction you have renamed a “struggle” because calling it sin would require repentance.
One compromise everybody thinks you abandoned.
One version of yourself that appears at church...
and another version that comes alive when nobody is watching.
Maybe your parents do not know.
Your spouse does not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your children do not know.
Your Facebook friends certainly do not know.
But Christ knows.
And here is where the Gospel changes the direction of this article.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that good people managed to keep their families spotless.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
The Bible contains fractured families because the Bible tells the truth about humanity.
Abraham's household was complicated.
Isaac's household was divided by favoritism.
Jacob's household would become painfully dysfunctional.
The family through which the promises moved was not a museum of flawless people.
It was filled with sinners who desperately needed grace.
And ultimately, the hope of Scripture does not rest on Isaac.
It does not rest on Jacob.
It certainly does not rest on Esau.
It rests on Jesus Christ.
When the angel announced His birth, Matthew explains His name:

“Thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.”
—Matthew 1:21, KJV
The Greek says:
αὐτὸς γὰρ σώσει τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν
autos gar sōsei ton laon autou apo tōn hamartiōn autōn
“For He Himself will save His people from their sins.”
That is the center.
Not merely better decisions.
Not religious image management.
Not becoming respectable enough that your parents stop worrying.
Salvation from sin through Christ.
Jesus did not come merely to improve the reputation of broken people.
He came to save sinners.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And because He lives, repentance is not the funeral of your hope.
It can become the doorway home.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia for repentance: a genuine turning of mind and heart that results in a changed direction.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling terrible about consequences.
Esau's story warns us that sorrow and spiritual transformation are not automatically the same thing.
You can cry because something hurt without surrendering the thing that is destroying you.
You can regret what happened without turning toward God.
You can hate the consequences and still secretly love the sin.
The Gospel calls us deeper.
Jesus does not say, “Hide it better.”
He calls sinners to come into the light.
He does not say, “Repair your image.”
He offers forgiveness.
He does not say, “Pretend you were never dirty.”
He cleanses.
And Scripture gives this astonishing promise:

“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
Maybe this is where the article stopped being about Esau.
Maybe somewhere between his appetite, his marriages, his parents' grief, and his attempt to repair things, you saw your own reflection.
Then do not hide from it.
Run to Christ.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction drives the sinner toward the mercy of God.
The Gospel does not expose your darkness so Jesus can stand at a distance and mock you.
Christ calls sinners out of darkness because He is light.
And perhaps the most dangerous thing you could do after reading this is simply scroll to the next post.
Do not turn conviction into entertainment.
Stop for a moment.
Ask yourself:
What have I been treating as light that God calls weighty?
What appetite has been making decisions for me?
Whose heart has my rebellion been wounding?
What have I been trying to fix externally while refusing to surrender internally?
And most importantly:
Have I actually brought this to Jesus?
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But you also do not have to keep pretending.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer desperately needed tonight.

Not because saving a post makes anyone holy, but because there may come a night when appetite becomes louder than conviction, and you need to remember what Esau's story teaches: do not trade what is weighty for what is immediate.

Supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping biblical teaching reach farther, but do not confuse supporting a ministry with glorifying God itself. We glorify God through Christ-centered faith, worship, obedience, love, generosity, witness, and lives surrendered to Him.
But before you leave, remember the two verses that began this entire journey.
Esau made his choices.
Isaac and Rebekah carried grief.
A family felt the consequences.
And yet the Bible continued moving toward something greater than their dysfunction.
Toward Bethlehem.
Toward Calvary.
Toward an empty tomb.
Toward Jesus.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final identity.
Your scandal may explain part of your story.
Your sin may have consequences.
Repentance may require painful honesty.
Reconciliation may take time.
Some earthly consequences may remain.
But for the sinner who comes to Christ, shame does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
So do not sell tomorrow's inheritance for tonight's appetite.
Do not keep decorating what Christ is asking you to surrender.
Do not spend another year trying to look healed when Jesus is inviting you to become honest.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive His grace.
And follow Christ.
Because perhaps the most unforgettable truth hidden behind this painful family scene is this:
The choices that broke hearts do not have more power than the Savior who transforms hearts.
